To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
aminoacyl-3′-adenines are inhibitors of protein synthesis.
the inhibition of protein synthesis by the antibiotic puromycin can be mimicked by aminoacyl-2′-adenosines.
aminoacyl-3′-adenosylenes, which are the 3′-terminal nucleotides of aminoacyl-tRNA, can inhibit protein synthesis in a manner comparable with that of puromycine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and properties of aminoacyl 5'-adenosines.
the synthesis of aminoacyl-3′-(2′)-adenosines and their effects on amino acid incorporation.
the inhibition of protein synthesis in E. coli by aminoacyl-3′-adenine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

leucyl- and aminoacyl-3′-adenines are inhibitors of protein synthesis, and that their inhibitory action is due to the formation of a complex between the 3′-terminal adenosine residue of the aminoacyl-sRNAs and the 3′ terminus of peptidyl-tRNA.
leucyl- and phenylalanyladenosines are inhibitors of protein synthesis, and that the aminoacyl residue of leucyladenosine does not confer specificity of inhibition.
leucyl- and other aminoacyl-3′-adenylates are puromycin-like analogues which inhibit protein synthesis by a mechanism similar to that of puomycin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aminoacyl-3′-adenine (AAd) analogues are inhibitors of protein synthesis.
the inhibition of aminoacyl-tRNA binding and/or translocation of aminoacyl tRNA on the ribosome, and the subsequent release of poly P, are the major effects of leucyl adenine.
aminoacyl-3'-(2)-adenosine is an effective inhibitor of protein synthesis, but its aminoacyl moiety is not responsible for the specificity of inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leucyl 2′-adenosin e and phenylalanyl 3′- and 2′-adeno sine inhibit protein synthesis in a similar fashion as puromycin.

the inhibition of protein synthesis by leucyl 2′-adenosines and tyrosyl 3′-(2′)-adenosine is due to their ability to interact with the ribosomes and not to their ability to act as analogs of aminoacyl sRNA.
leucyl- and phenylalanyladenosines, as well as puromycin, can inhibit protein synthesis by binding to the A-site of the ribosome and thus competing for the same ribosomal site.
